summary: The Omoda 9 SHS is Chery's flagship in Australia and is sold here in a single MY27 Virtue AWD grade, listed by Omoda at $58,990 (reviewers still quote the $61,990 launch price), pairing a 1.5-litre turbo petrol with three electric motors for 395kW, a 4.9-second 0-100km/h claim and 145km of WLTP electric range from a 34.46kWh battery — roughly double the electric range of a BYD Sealion 6 or Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV for similar money. Australian reviewers are consistent that the powertrain, equipment list and cabin quality are the strongest part of the car and that the chassis is not: CarExpert, CarsGuide, Chasing Cars and carsales all criticise vague steering, loose body control and a busy, head-tossing ride, and none rates it as a genuine premium drive. It is a compelling equipment-and-range package with a hard ceiling on driving polish, and with no resale history in a brand that launched here in 2025.
pros: 145km of WLTP electric-only range from a 34.46kWh battery — around double a BYD Sealion 6 Premium AWD (81km) or a Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV, and enough that most Melbourne buyers would rarely start the engine
395kW/650Nm from a 1.5-litre turbo petrol and three motors gives a claimed 4.9-second 0-100km/h, quicker than any PHEV SUV near the price and quicker than most $100k performance SUVs
70kW DC fast charging (30-80 per cent in about 25 minutes) plus 6.6kW AC — the Sealion 6 and Outlander PHEV have no DC capability at all, so an Omoda 9 can top up its electric range on a road trip

Eight-year/unlimited-kilometre vehicle warranty with a matching eight-year/unlimited-kilometre high-voltage battery warranty guaranteeing at least 70 per cent residual capacity, plus eight years of capped-price servicing ($3343 total) and roadside assistance

1500kg braked towing where the Jaecoo J7 SHS has no braked tow rating at all, and a 471-litre boot to the window line (660 litres to the roof) against the J7 SHS's 340 litres to the cargo cover — though the seven-seat Chery Tiggo 9 and Jaecoo J8 carry more once their third rows are folded
cons: Charge-sustaining economy is nothing like the 1.4L/100km NEDC label: CompleteCar puts a depleted battery at about 7.0L/100km, AutoTrader NZ saw 6.0-6.9L/100km and km77's 120km/h motorway loop 8.2L/100km — a 2.2-tonne AWD SUV on 95-octane premium, so the running-cost case collapses for anyone who cannot charge at home

Ride and steering are the near-universal complaint: CarExpert calls it a 'bouncy, head-tossing ride', CarsGuide marks it down for 'vague steering' and 'lacking body control', and Chasing Cars describes the steering as 'numb and lifeless' — it does not drive like the premium car its price and equipment imply
Five seats only, where a Chery Tiggo 8 Super Hybrid at $42,990 and several rivals at this money seat seven, and the front seats lack height and tilt adjustment despite being power-operated

Omoda launched in Australia in 2025 with one model and a small dealer network, and the advertised price keeps resetting — from $61,990 at launch to $58,990 on Omoda's MY27 configurator, alongside gift-card and 1.88 per cent finance campaigns — so resale is unproven, which is why a steeper-than-average depreciation curve is assumed here

Only one grade is offered, so there is no cheaper way into the nameplate: the choice is $58,990 or nothing, roughly $21,000 above the closely related Jaecoo J7 SHS Track, and the boot is only mid-sized for a 4.78m SUV once measured to the window line rather than the roof
